title: Your Wallet Can't Hold a Week of Kip. Here's How Expats in Laos Actually Pay.
summary: Living in Laos without a local bank account? Here's how expats use LAO QR codes in Vientiane and Luang Prabang to skip ATM fees and the kip-stuffed wallet problem.
body_markdown:
Pull out enough cash for a normal week in Laos and you'll understand the problem immediately. Kip comes in big denominations, prices run into the hundreds of thousands for ordinary things, and your wallet goes from flat to bursting after one ATM visit. A coffee, a bowl of khao piak sen, a Loca ride, a water refill, and you're already peeling through a stack of notes.


Meanwhile the ATM that gave you that stack capped your withdrawal at a frustratingly low amount and charged you a fee for the privilege. Do that twice a week and you're paying a recurring tax just to hold paper.


Expats who settle into Vientiane or Luang Prabang figure out fast that there's a better system hiding in plain sight, and it's taped to almost every counter.


## The LAO QR sticker is the whole story


Laos has a national QR payment standard called LAO QR. It's the laminated square you see at coffee shops on Setthathirath Road, at minimarts, at the night market stalls in Luang Prabang, at pharmacies, even at some temple donation boxes. Locals scan it with their banking apps ([BCEL One](https://moretapay.com/networks/onepay) is the one you'll see on everyone's phone) and pay in seconds.


Watch the counter at any Vientiane cafe for five minutes. The person ahead of you doesn't reach for a wallet. They scan, show the confirmation screen, and walk out. Nobody counts change. Nobody waits while the vendor digs for small notes.


The catch for foreigners has always been the same one: those local apps want a Lao bank account, and opening one as an expat involves paperwork, patience, and often a long-term visa you may not have yet.


## You don't need the local bank, just a way into the QR


This is where the setup gets simple. Moreta Pay lets you scan the same LAO QR codes locals use, without a Lao bank account. You top up a wallet from your home bank before or after you arrive (US banks via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card), keep the balance in your own currency, and convert only when you actually pay.


At the counter it works like this:


1. Open the app and scan the merchant's LAO QR sticker.


2. Check the merchant name, the amount in kip, and the exact FX rate on screen.


3. Confirm. The vendor's phone pings, you're done.


No ATM run first. No mental math on six-digit prices while a queue forms behind you. No wondering what your home bank quietly added on top. The rate you see before you confirm is the rate you get.


## What a cashless day in Vientiane looks like


Morning coffee near the river: QR sticker at the register, scan and go. Lunch at a noodle shop: same. Groceries at a minimart: the cashier points at the sticker before you even ask. Evening Beerlao with friends at a riverside bar: one person scans, everyone else settles up later.


Luang Prabang is further along than first-time visitors expect. Guesthouses, cafes on the peninsula, the smoothie stands near the night market, plenty of them have LAO QR now, and vendors often prefer it because they don't have to break your 100,000 kip note at 8 a.m.


That last point matters more than it sounds. Change is a genuine friction in Laos. Hand over a large note for a small purchase and you'll sometimes get an apologetic shrug and a wait while someone runs next door. QR removes the whole negotiation.


## Where you still need paper


Honesty time: Laos is not cash-free, and pretending otherwise will strand you.


Keep kip on hand for village stops outside the cities, some tuk-tuk and songthaew drivers, small-town markets, alms-giving if you participate, and anywhere the power or mobile signal is flaky. Rural Laos runs on cash and will for a while.


The working formula most expats land on: QR for daily life in Vientiane and Luang Prabang, a modest cash reserve for everything else. That flips the ATM from a twice-weekly chore into a once-a-month errand, which also means you eat those withdrawal fees far less often.


It's the same pattern expats describe


[across the river in Thailand with PromptPay](https://moretapay.com/blog/no-thai-bank-account-yet-how-expats-actually-pay-for-daily-life-in-thailand-2026-11-14)


: digital for the routine stuff, a little cash as insurance, never a fat wallet.


## Bills, bookings, and the non-counter payments


Daily spending is half of expat life. The other half is the recurring stuff, and QR helps there too.


Booking a slow boat leg or a Vang Vieng guesthouse through Trip.com or Agoda? Those platforms support QR-based checkout, and Moreta Pay handles it the same way as a street-side sticker: scan, review, confirm. In supported countries you can pay bills through the app as well, which beats standing in line with an envelope of notes.


For rent, it depends on your landlord. Plenty still want cash or a Lao bank transfer, but a growing number in Vientiane will happily take a QR payment, especially younger landlords who already run their lives through their banking app. Ask. The answer is yes more often than it was even a year ago.


## Set yourself up before the plane lands


A short checklist, in order:


**Download and verify before you fly.**


Linking your home bank and verifying your identity is easiest on good wifi with your documents handy, not on arrival-day jet lag.


**Top up in your own currency.**


Your balance sits in dollars, euros, or pounds until the moment you pay, so you're not forced to guess how much kip to commit to upfront.


**Withdraw one sensible cash reserve.**


Accept the ATM fee once, keep the notes for rural trips and cash-only moments, and stop feeding the machine every few days.


**Scan your first QR somewhere low-stakes.**


A coffee or a market snack. Once you've seen the merchant name and FX rate pop up and the vendor's phone chime, the rest of your Laos spending gets boring in the best way.


One more sensible habit: lock your phone down properly, since it's now doing your wallet's job. We covered


[what actually happens to a QR payment app if your phone is stolen abroad](https://moretapay.com/blog/how-secure-is-a-qr-payment-app-abroad-once-your-phone-gets-stolen)


, and the short version is that a few minutes of setup makes a lost phone an annoyance instead of a crisis.


## The thin wallet test


Here's how you'll know the system is working: a month in, your wallet is thin again. The kip in it is a reserve, not a daily supply. You haven't memorized the ATM locations near your apartment because you barely use them. Paying for lunch takes four seconds and you saw the exact exchange rate before you tapped confirm.


That's the version of Laos expat life worth setting up. If you're heading to Vientiane or Luang Prabang without a local bank account,

and start scanning the same stickers everyone around you already uses.
